content: Oily fish, also known as oil-rich fish or pelagic fish, are characterized by the presence of oils distributed throughout their fillets and within the belly cavity surrounding the gut. This is in contrast to white fish, where oils are primarily concentrated in the liver. The fillets of oily fish can contain up to 30% oil, although this percentage varies both within and between species. These fish typically inhabit the pelagic zones of the oceans. Oily fish are an excellent source of vitamins A and D, as well as omega-3 fatty acids, which are known for their numerous health benefits. Consequently, the consumption of oily fish is considered more advantageous for human health compared to white fish. Research suggests that omega-3 fatty acids in oily fish may alleviate symptoms of depression, reduce the risk of heart disease, and improve inflammatory conditions such as arthritis. Research on Dementia A French study published in 2002 in the British Medical Journal followed 1,674 elderly residents of southern France over a seven-year period. The study examined their dietary habits, specifically the consumption of meat versus seafood, and the presence of dementia symptoms. The findings indicated that individuals who consumed fish at least once a week had a significantly lower risk of being diagnosed with dementia over the seven-year period. However, the study could not definitively determine whether fish consumption protected against dementia or whether dementia itself reduced the participants' ability to consume fish. Additionally, individuals with higher levels of education were found to have a lower risk of dementia and a higher consumption of fish, though the relationship between these three factors remains unclear. Cardiovascular Health Consuming oily fish twice per week may help prevent sudden cardiac death caused by myocardial infarction by reducing the risk of cardiac arrhythmias. Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), a key component of fish oils, has been shown to significantly reduce inflammation by being converted into resolvins within the body. This anti-inflammatory effect is beneficial for both cardiovascular health and conditions such as arthritis. Recommended Consumption In 1994, the UK Committee on Medical Aspects of Food and Nutrition Policy (COMA) recommended that individuals consume at least two portions of fish per week, one of which should be oily fish. In 2004, the UK Food Standards Agency provided further guidance on the recommended minimum and maximum quantities of oily fish to balance the health benefits of omega-3 fatty acids against the potential risks of methylmercury (MeHg) exposure. For men, boys, and women beyond childbearing age, up to four portions (approximately 9 ounces) of oily fish per week are recommended. For women of childbearing age, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, and for girls, up to two portions per week are advised. There is no recommended limit on the consumption of white fish. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the USDA have set guidelines (as of 2007) limiting the consumption of fatty fish with methylmercury levels exceeding one part per million. Fish such as tilefish, king mackerel, shark, and swordfish, as well as some locally caught fish, fall into this category. Pregnant or nursing women and children under the age of six should completely avoid high-MeHg fish and limit their intake of moderateand low-MeHg fish to 12 ounces per week. Albacore tuna should be limited to 6 ounces or less per week for these populations. Oils from Fish and Plant Sources as Omega-3 Fatty Acid Alternatives Concerns regarding contamination, dietary preferences, or limited supply have prompted investigations into plant-based sources of omega-3 fatty acids, such as flaxseed and hempseed oil. Studies have shown that lactating women who supplemented their diets with flaxseed oil experienced increases in blood and breast milk concentrations of alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). However, no changes were observed in the concentrations of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).
